sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.body: This Geotechnical Engineering Circular (GEC) coalesces more than four decades of research, development and practical experience in the application of shallow foundations for support of transportation structures. The document is intended to be a definitive desk reference for the transportation professional responsible for design, procurement and construction of shallow foundations for bridges and other transportation-related structures. This GEC draws heavily from previous published work by FHWA, State (and Local) Highway Agencies (SHAs) and other authors of practical guidance related to shallow foundations. It is intended to provide a single reference source for state-of-the-practice information on the design and construction of shallow foundations. Special attention has been given to case histories and design examples on the use of shallow foundations to support abutments in compacted approach embankments.
key_points: Consolidates four decades of research and practice for shallow foundation design
Intended as a definitive desk reference for transportation professionals
Draws from FHWA, SHA, and other published guidance sources
Provides state-of-the-practice information as a single reference source
Special emphasis on shallow foundations bearing on compacted structural fills
Includes case histories for abutments supported in compacted approach embankments
sections.applicability: Design, procurement, and construction of shallow foundations for bridges and transportation-related structures.

sections.title: Background
sections.body: Shallow foundations represent the simplest form of load transfer from a structure to the ground beneath. They are typically constructed with generally small excavations, do not require specialized construction equipment or tools, and are relatively inexpensive. In most cases, shallow foundations are the most cost-effective choice for support of a structure. Bridges, however, are frequently supported on deep foundations such as driven piling, largely due to continued use of past practice rooted in railroad construction. In many cases, pile support of transportation structures is wise, if not essential, where waterway crossings demand protection from scour, poor ground conditions exist, or transient load conditions such as vessel impact or seismicity are present. However, many transportation bridges are associated with upland development and interchanges on competent ground. The combination of good, competent ground conditions and an available source of good-quality, granular fill material should be seen as an opportunity to save bridge construction costs. Cost savings from supporting bridge abutments within compacted approach fills include: shortened construction schedule, deletion of piles through compacted fill to competent foundation materials, and reduction in concrete and steel materials costs. Key research findings: (1) approximately 600,000 highway bridges in the US with average replacement cost of $500,000; shallow foundations can be constructed for 50 to 65 percent of the cost of deep foundations (Briaud & Gibbens, 1995); (2) WSDOT constructed more than 500 highway bridges between 1965 and 1980 with one or more abutments or piers supported on spread footings (DiMillio, 1982); (3) FHWA research on 21 bridge foundations on cohesionless soil showed 70 percent of settlement occurred prior to bridge deck placement, with average post-deck settlement less than 6 mm (Gifford et al., 1987). Conclusions: sufficient financial incentive exists to promote shallow foundations where feasible; shallow foundation support of bridges has a proven track record on hundreds of projects; sufficient performance data exist to alleviate concerns over settlement performance where good ground conditions exist.
key_points: Shallow foundations are the simplest and most cost-effective load transfer mechanism
Bridge foundations on piles are often driven by past practice rather than engineering necessity
Shallow foundations cost 50-65% of deep foundations (Briaud & Gibbens, 1995)
WSDOT built 500+ bridges on spread footings between 1965-1980 (DiMillio, 1982)
FHWA research showed 70% of settlement occurs before deck placement; post-deck settlement averages less than 6 mm
Pile support is essential where scour, poor ground, vessel impact, or seismicity are concerns
Upland bridge sites with competent ground and good granular fill are ideal candidates for shallow foundations
sections.applicability: Evaluation of whether shallow foundations are appropriate versus deep foundations for bridge and transportation structures, particularly at sites with competent ground conditions.

sections.title: Relevant Publications
sections.body: Although the Shallow Foundations GEC is intended to be a stand-alone reference document, additional detail and background on the methods and procedures can be found in the following publications: AASHTO Standard Specifications for Highway Bridges, 16th Edition (AASHTO, 1996); AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications, 2nd Edition (AASHTO, 1998); NHI 13212 Soils and Foundations Workshop Reference Manual (Cheney & Chassie, 2000); NHI 132037 Shallow Foundations Workshop Reference Manual (Munfakh et al., 2000); NHI 132031 Subsurface Investigation Workshop Reference Manual (Arman et al., 1997); NHI 132035 Module 5 - Rock Slopes: Design, Excavation and Stabilization (Wyllie & Mah, 1998); Foundation Engineering Handbook (Fang, 1991); Soil Mechanics (Lambe & Whitman, 1969); Rock Slope Engineering (Hoek & Bray, 1981).
key_points: GEC is designed as a stand-alone reference but supplements other key publications
AASHTO Standard Specifications (16th Ed.) and LRFD Bridge Design Specifications (2nd Ed.) are primary design codes
NHI 132037 is the companion Shallow Foundations Workshop Reference Manual
NHI 13212 covers general soils and foundations; NHI 132031 covers subsurface investigation
Rock slope references (NHI 132035, Hoek & Bray 1981) provide guidance for foundations on rock
sections.applicability: Reference list for practitioners needing additional detail beyond this GEC on shallow foundation design methods and subsurface investigation.

sections.title: Shallow Foundation Systems Applications
sections.body: Shallow foundations principally distribute structural loads over large areas of near-surface soil or rock to lower the intensity of the applied loads to levels tolerable for the foundation soils. Shallow foundations are used in many applications in highway projects when the subsurface conditions are appropriate. Such applications include bridge abutments on soil slopes or embankments, bridge intermediate piers, retaining walls, culverts, sign posts, noise barriers, and rest stop or maintenance building foundations. Footings or mats may support column loads under buildings. Bridge piers are often supported on shallow foundations using various structural configurations.
key_points: Shallow foundations distribute loads over large areas to reduce bearing stress intensity
Applications include bridge abutments, intermediate piers, retaining walls, culverts, sign posts, and noise barriers
Also used for rest stop and maintenance building foundations
Footings or mats may support column loads under buildings
Subsurface conditions must be appropriate for shallow foundation use
sections.applicability: All highway project applications where near-surface soil or rock conditions can support structural loads at tolerable stress levels.
